claims.text: The starting material consists of refractory-alloy powders mixed with a binder to form a printable ink.
A refractory-alloy green part can be fabricated by 3D ink-extrusion printing.
The ink-extrusion printing step is performed at room temperature.
Forming the green part by 3D ink-extrusion printing reduces the required sintering temperature.
3D ink-extrusion printing produces a highly porous green structure.
The printed green structure has enhanced contact among powder particles.
The porous printed microstructure has a high specific surface area.
The printed microstructure reduces diffusion distances between particles.
Enhanced particle contact lowers the activation energy required for densification.
Lowering the activation energy for densification reduces the necessary sintering temperature.
Printed samples can attain densification comparable to conventionally pressed powders at a lower sintering temperature.
Printed samples can attain mechanical properties comparable to conventionally pressed powders at a lower sintering temperature.
Conventionally prepared powder compacts require higher sintering temperatures for full densification.
The achievable temperature reduction depends on powder composition, binder type, green density, and binder-burnout efficiency.
The cited evidence supports formation of a porous green structure by 3D ink-extrusion methods.
The exact sintering-temperature reduction and its universality across refractory-alloy systems remain uncertain.
